Linguist says there are over 7000 languages in the world.
At the popular end of the spectrum, x billion that speaks mandarin, y billion that speaks hindu hindu, at the rare end of the spectrum, there are z who speak A language and zz for B language. Below is the distribution of language as the number of speakers.

On average, a language is spoken by 100000X people, but is that informative? We could look at the variance @sec-variance  and then the standard deviation and realize that it is highly variable (as seen by the two spectrum above.). If we use the median (see below on how to compute that), the summary statistic is about 1000 speaker per langauge.
Which number do you find more useful? If you are some how wants to protect the language, you might use the median and says that about 3500 languages are spoken by less than a 1000 people. And if you want to you might use the mean.

The major connundrum is whether one should use the mean or the mediane to compare two distribution (as this is incomplete (see @sec-mean)). But Being more informed will allow a more informed decision.

## Formal {.unnumbered}
<!-- The definition of the median transitions from a simple algorithmic sorting rule in applied statistics to a more sophisticated optimization and probability criteria in theoretical statistics.
Here are the rigorous definitions for both, complete with textbook sources and raw LaTeX formatting. -->

1. Applied Statistics: The Sample Median
<!-- In applied data analysis, the median is an empirical descriptive statistic of central tendency. It is defined as the middle value when the data points are ordered from smallest to largest. Because of this, its exact formula changes depending on whether the sample size n is odd or even.

Textbook Source
Book: Introductory Statistics (10th Edition)
Author: Neil A. Weiss
Publisher: Pearson -->

The Definition
In Chapter 3 ("Descriptive Measures"), Weiss defines the sample median rigorously based on sample size positioning:
"Arrange the data in increasing order.
If the number of observations (n) is odd, the median is the observation exactly in the middle of the ordered list.
If the number of observations (n) is even, the median is the mean of the two middle observations in the ordered list.
In other words, if the ordered observations are denoted
$x_{(1)},x_{(2)}, \ldots, x_{(n)}$
​
, the median $\tilde{X}$ is

$\tilde{x} = \begin{cases} x_{\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)} & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \\ \frac{1}{2}\left(x_{\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)} + x_{\left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right)}\right) & \text{if } n \text{ is even} \end{cases}$

## Examples {.unnumbered}
The same mediane for the following data
 1.  1, 1, 3, 3, 3;
 2.  1, 2, 3, 4, 5;
 3.  1, 3, 3, 10, 1000.
 4.  -100, 1, 3, 3, 5

The median of

 1.  1, 1, 3, 3: 2
 2.  1, 2, 3, 4: 2.5
 3.  1, 3, 3, 10: 3
 4.  -100, 1, 3, 3: 2.5

If you ever do by hand sort by smallest to largest and go halfway. Of course work for few numbers but uncessary for larger one.

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- The major advantage of a median over a mean is that it is less to extreme values or outliers. It is up to one's judgement if that is or not.
- If uncertain, maybe compute both mean and median (one line in R) as an exploration and see how much they differ and how that will affect your conclusion.
- Another example of picking a single number, now three as measure of central tendency (mean, mode, mediane). As we progress, we are already more informed in which one to choose. But there are also more and more metrics to report our data.
- Median is simply the 50% quantile @sec-quantile.
- And as we are more informed, we could also make more honest and deliberate. While it can allow to fool people (hoopefully enough consious), better it allows you to be less fooled,

1. Theoretical Statistics: The Distribution Median
In theoretical statistics, the median of a random variable X is defined as any real number m that splits the probability distribution into two equal halves of at least 50%. It is rigorously formalized using inequalities containing the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF).

Textbook Source
Book: Statistical Inference (2nd Edition, 2002)
Authors: George Casella and Roger L. Berger
Publisher: Duxbury / Thomson Learning

The Definition
In Chapter 2 ("Fractional Populations and Medians"), Casella and Berger present the unifying probability definition that accounts for both discrete and continuous distributions:
"A median of a random variable X is a real number m satisfying
$P(X \le m) \ge \frac{1}{2} \quad \text{and} \quad P(X \ge m) \ge \frac{1}{2}$"

The Continuous Case Simplification
As the authors point out, if X is a continuous random variable with a continuous CDF FX(x), the inequalities collapse into a single strict equation:
$F_X(m) = \int_{-\infty}^{m} f(x) \, dx = \frac{1}{2}$

1. The Theoretical "Optimization" Definition
Advanced mathematical statistics textbooks also define the theoretical median as the absolute distance minimizer. While the population mean minimizes the expected squared error, the population median minimizes the expected absolute error.

Textbook Source
Book: Mathematical Statistics (2nd Edition, 2003)
Author: Jun Shao
Publisher: Springer Science & Business Media

The Definition
In Chapter 1, when discussing properties of parameters, the median is defined as an optimization solution:
"A median of X (or of its distribution PX
​) is any constant m that minimizes the expected absolute loss:
$\mathbb{E}|X - m|$
"
Formally, this can be written using optimization notation:
$m = \operatorname{argmin}_{c} \mathbb{E}|X - c|$ -->
